text: `sudo systemctl status notify-relay.socket` shows `active (listening)`, and `sudo systemctl status notify-relay.service` shows `inactive (dead)` waiting to be triggered -- that's the normal, healthy state for a socket-activated service that hasn't received a connection yet. Neither unit is 'broken' on its own. So check what actually happens when something connects at the documented path: `curl --unix-socket /run/notify-relay.sock --max-time 5 http://localhost/`.

That times out / gets connection refused, even though the socket unit is definitely listening on *something*. Check exactly what path it's bound to: `sudo systemctl show notify-relay.socket -p Listen`, or read it straight from the unit: `sudo systemctl cat notify-relay.socket`.

The `ListenStream=` value is `/tmp/notify-relay.sock`, not `/run/notify-relay.sock` -- moved there during a migration that never updated the clients or docs. Confirm the service really does work, just at the wrong address: `curl --unix-socket /tmp/notify-relay.sock http://localhost/` answers fine.

Fix the path in `/etc/systemd/system/notify-relay.socket`'s `ListenStream=` back to `/run/notify-relay.sock`. A socket's bound address can't be changed by a reload alone -- stop it first so the old socket is released, then reload and start: `sudo systemctl stop notify-relay.socket && sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl start notify-relay.socket`. Confirm with `curl --unix-socket /run/notify-relay.sock http://localhost/`.
